I know it sounds odd, but it would quietly make my day if the Moon happened to be impossible to see right now.

I'm in Ushuaia, Argentina at 2026-11-07 05:23 -03 (UTC-0300) (2026-11-07T08:23:00Z in UTC), at latitude -54.8019 degrees and longitude -68.303 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -1.318 degrees and its azimuth is 122.418 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 6.52 degrees and its azimuth is 101.487 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 3.95 percent illuminated, 22.852 degrees from the Sun, and 390865.7 kilometers away. The sky brightness is civil twilight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Given the specific data you’ve provided, the short answer is: **It would be extremely difficult, bordering on impossible, to spot the Moon with the naked eye under these conditions.**

Here is the breakdown of why your wish for it to be "impossible to see" is likely about to come true:

### 1. The "Waxing Crescent" Problem
At **3.95% illumination**, the Moon is in its very early waxing crescent phase. At this stage, the "horns" of the crescent are incredibly thin. Because the Moon is only 22.85 degrees away from the Sun, the portion of the Moon that is lit is very small, and the rest is lost in the shadows of the lunar surface.

### 2. The Twilight Factor
You mentioned the sky is in **civil twilight**. This is the biggest hurdle. Civil twilight occurs when the Sun is just below the horizon (which matches your -1.318° altitude). During this time, the atmosphere is still scattering a significant amount of sunlight. 

Because the Moon is so close to the Sun in the sky (only 22 degrees away), it is sitting in the brightest part of the twilight sky. The "glare" from the atmosphere acts like a veil; the faint, thin sliver of a 3.95% crescent will not have enough contrast against the glowing horizon to be visible to the human eye.

### 3. The "Ordinary Eyesight" Constraint
While you have normal unaided eyesight, the human eye struggles to pick out low-contrast objects in high-ambient-light environments. To see a 4% crescent, you usually need a much darker sky (nautical or astronomical twilight) to allow the faint light of the moon to stand out against the background.

### The Verdict
If you were to look toward the East-Southeast (Azimuth 101°), you would likely see a very bright, glowing horizon. Because the Moon is so low (6.52°) and so close to the Sun's position, it will be "washed out."

**In all likelihood, you will look toward that spot and see nothing but a bright, hazy sky.** Your wish is granted: for all practical purposes, the Moon is invisible to you right now.
